title: CSC2770 Module 6: The OSI Model (Layers 7, 6, 5)
source: "Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) Model" slides, Jacob Strickler, CSC 2770: Introduction to Systems and Networking (adapted from Mr. Eric Brown and Dr. Mike Rogers)

questions.q: Which organization created the OSI model?
choices: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)
questions.explain: The ISO created the OSI. ISO is the organization and OSI is the model. The acronyms are easy to swap, so keep them straight.

questions.q: What does the acronym OSI stand for, as in the OSI model?
questions.explain: OSI = Open Systems Interconnection. The ISO created it to help people understand and standardize networking.

questions.q: How many layers does the OSI model divide networking architecture into?
questions.explain: Seven layers: 7 Application, 6 Presentation, 5 Session, 4 Transport, 3 Network, 2 Data Link, 1 Physical.

questions.q: Which list gives the OSI layers in order from Layer 7 down to Layer 1?
choices: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical
Application, Session, Presentation, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical
Application, Presentation, Session, Network, Transport, Data Link, Physical
Application, Presentation, Transport, Session, Network, Physical, Data Link
questions.explain: Top down: Application (7), Presentation (6), Session (5), Transport (4), Network (3), Data Link (2), Physical (1). One mnemonic: All People Seem To Need Data Processing.

questions.q: Which layer sits directly below the Session Layer?
questions.explain: Session is Layer 5, so the layer directly below it is Layer 4, Transport. Presentation (6) is directly above it.

questions.q: What layer number is the Presentation Layer?
questions.explain: Presentation is Layer 6. It sits between Application (7) and Session (5).

questions.q: OSI layers are numbered from the top down, so the Application Layer is Layer 1.
questions.explain: Numbering starts at the bottom: Physical is Layer 1 and Application is Layer 7, the topmost layer.

questions.q: Getting data from one computer to another involves many separate jobs. Which of these are among them?
choices: Physically connecting cables or other media
Maintaining security of data in transit
Compiling source code into machine instructions
Allocating CPU time between running processes
questions.explain: Networking involves connecting media, packaging information, telling devices apart, finding optimal paths, checking for errors, keeping data secure in transit, and unpacking data at the destination. Compiling code and CPU scheduling are not networking jobs.

questions.q: Why does the OSI model split networking into layers?
choices: Networking involves many jobs; each layer handles its own part
Each layer must run on its own separate physical device
Layers let all network traffic share a single protocol
Layering is required so data can be encrypted at every step
questions.explain: Networking is complicated. Treating it as one problem would be unmanageable, so the model divides the work into levels and gives each level its own job.

questions.q: The Application Layer (Layer 7) handles communication between:
choices: Two network cards over a physical cable
Routers choosing paths across the internet
The CPU and main memory of one computer
questions.explain: Layer 7 connects end-user applications (the programs you interact with) to the network. It involves some kind of user interface plus protocols that let the application communicate over the network.

questions.q: Which of these are services at the Application Layer?
questions.explain: Application Layer services: web browsing, email, file transfer and remote access. Data compression belongs to the Presentation Layer (6). Negotiating duplex belongs to the Session Layer (5).

questions.q: Which protocol is used to retrieve content such as HTML pages and images from web servers?
questions.explain: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) retrieves web content such as HTML pages and images, which is what makes web browsing possible.

questions.q: Which protocol sends email from clients to mail servers, or between mail servers?
questions.explain: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) sends email from a client to a mail server, or from one mail server to another.

questions.q: Which protocol provides remote access and command over another machine, with its traffic encrypted?
questions.explain: SSH (Secure Shell) gives encrypted remote access to another machine and lets you run commands on it.

questions.q: Which protocol is optimized for navigating, uploading, and downloading raw files?
questions.explain: FTP (File Transfer Protocol) transfers files from client to server and is optimized for navigating, uploading and downloading raw files.

questions.q: What does SMTP stand for?
questions.explain: SMTP = Simple Mail Transfer Protocol. It sends email.

questions.q: What does SSH stand for?
questions.explain: SSH = Secure Shell, used for encrypted remote access and command of another machine.

questions.q: FTPS and SFTP are security-enhanced variants of which protocol?
questions.explain: FTPS and SFTP are security-enhanced versions of FTP that add encryption. HTTPS plays the same role for HTTP.

questions.q: SSH needs a separate security-enhanced variant (the way HTTP has HTTPS) because SSH traffic is not encrypted.
questions.explain: SSH traffic is already encrypted, which is the 'Secure' in Secure Shell. HTTP and FTP are the protocols with added-encryption variants (HTTPS, FTPS, SFTP).

questions.q: In principle, emails and web pages could just be sent as file transfers over FTP. Why do SMTP and HTTP exist anyway?
choices: Each protocol is designed and optimized for its own context
FTP can only send files from a server down to a client
Each OSI layer is required to have exactly one protocol
SMTP and HTTP are faster because they skip the network
questions.explain: Each protocol is optimized for its own context. SMTP is formatted for email and handles recipients and attachments. HTTP delivers information in a browser-friendly format. FTP is optimized for working with raw files.

questions.q: In the HTTP request line 'GET / HTTP/1.1', what is 'GET'?
questions.explain: A request line has the form Method, Path, Protocol version. GET is the method, meaning 'retrieve this resource'.

questions.q: In the HTTP request line 'GET / HTTP/1.1', what is '/'?
questions.explain: '/' is the path, meaning which resource on the server is wanted. '/' is the root (the home page).

questions.q: In the HTTP response line 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK', what is '200'?
questions.explain: A response line has the form Protocol version, Status code, Status message. 200 is the status code, and it means success.

questions.q: In the HTTP response line 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK', what is the part 'OK' called?
questions.explain: 'OK' is the status message, the human-readable text that goes with status code 200.

questions.q: What is the order of the parts in the first line of an HTTP response?
choices: Protocol version, status code, status message
Status code, status message, protocol version
Status message, status code, protocol version
questions.explain: Response: Protocol version, Status code, Status message (e.g. HTTP/1.1 200 OK). 'Method, path, protocol version' is the order of a request line.

questions.q: What is the order of the parts in the first line of an HTTP request?
choices: Protocol version, status code, status message
questions.explain: Request: Method, Path, Protocol version (e.g. GET / HTTP/1.1). A response starts with the protocol version instead.

questions.q: An HTTP request contains the lines 'Host: developer.mozilla.org' and 'Accept-Language: fr'. What are these lines?
questions.explain: They are headers, which carry extra information about the request. Here they name the site and say the client would like French.

questions.q: An HTTP response includes the header 'content-type: text/html'. What does it tell the client?
choices: The response body is an HTML document
The client must reply with an HTML form
The page may be cached for one hour
The server only accepts text in French
questions.explain: content-type describes what kind of data the body holds. text/html means the body is an HTML page.

questions.q: An HTTP response header reads 'cache-control: public, max-age=3600'. max-age is given in seconds. How many minutes is that?
questions.explain: 3600 seconds / 60 = 60 minutes, or 1 hour, which is how long the response may be cached.

questions.q: An HTTP request line begins with the protocol version, followed by a status code.
questions.explain: That is the form of a response line (HTTP/1.1 200 OK). A request line begins with the method, then the path, then the protocol version (GET / HTTP/1.1).

questions.q: Which of these are responsibilities of the Presentation Layer?
questions.explain: Presentation Layer = Translate, Compress, Encrypt. Authentication and duplex negotiation belong to the Session Layer (5).

questions.q: Where does the Presentation Layer get its name?
choices: It deals with the form in which data is presented
It presents the user interface for applications
It presents a device's identity to the network
It presents data to the physical cable for sending
questions.explain: Layer 6 deals with the form in which data is presented, hence the name. The user interface is part of the Application Layer (7).

questions.q: Why is data translation needed?
choices: Not all systems represent data in the same way
Data must be made smaller before it is sent
Data must be unreadable to anyone but the recipient
The two devices must agree who talks and when
questions.explain: Different systems represent data differently, so data has to be translatable across systems for the receiver to understand what the sender sent.

questions.q: Which character encoding is used by older IBM systems and is completely different from ASCII?
questions.explain: Older IBM systems use EBCDIC, while most modern systems use ASCII or Unicode. Text has to be translated (for example ASCII to EBCDIC) when it moves between them.

questions.q: What does EBCDIC stand for?
answer: Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code
extended binary coded decimal interchange code
questions.explain: EBCDIC = Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code, the character encoding used by older IBM systems.

questions.q: Besides character encoding, which other difference between systems shows that data translation is needed?
choices: Byte order: Little Endian vs. Big Endian
Duplex: full duplex vs. half duplex
Media: copper cable vs. fiber optic
questions.explain: Some systems are Little Endian and others are Big Endian. If the receiver assumes the wrong byte order, it reads the wrong value, so the data has to be translated.

questions.q: The 32-bit value 0x12345678 is stored on a Little Endian system. Which bytes appear in memory, from lowest address to highest?
questions.explain: Little Endian stores the least significant byte first: 78 56 34 12. Big Endian stores the most significant byte first: 12 34 56 78.

questions.q: A modern PC sends ASCII text to an old IBM mainframe, and the mainframe displays garbage characters. Which Presentation Layer responsibility was not handled?
questions.explain: ASCII and EBCDIC store the same characters as different bit patterns. Translation makes sure data sent by one system can be understood by the other.

questions.q: Which of these describes data encryption?
choices: Converting data into an unreadable format the intended recipient can reverse
Removing less important data so the file is smaller and quicker to send
Verifying the identity of a user or device before an exchange begins
Converting characters from ASCII into EBCDIC so older systems can read them
questions.explain: Encryption improves security by making data unreadable to everyone except the intended recipient, who can reverse it. The other choices describe lossy compression, authentication and translation.

questions.q: Data encryption is one of the Session Layer's responsibilities.
questions.explain: Encryption is a Presentation Layer (6) responsibility, along with translation and compression. The Session Layer (5) manages sessions: authentication, authorization and conversation structure.

questions.q: How does compression optimize network communication?
choices: It reduces the number of bits that must be transmitted
It lets both endpoints transmit at the same time
It converts data into a format the receiver can read
It finds the shortest path between two devices
questions.explain: Compression cuts the number of bits that have to travel across the network, which makes communication more efficient.

questions.q: What do compression methods generally exploit to reduce the amount of data needed?
questions.explain: Methods vary, but they tend to use patterns to express the same thing with less data. RLE, for example, exploits runs of repeated symbols.

questions.q: Run Length Encoding (RLE) writes each run as a count followed by the symbol, so AAAAA becomes 5A. RLE-encode: WWWWWWBBBWWWW
questions.explain: The runs are WWWWWW (6), BBB (3), WWWW (4), giving 6W 3B 4W.

questions.q: Give the RLE encoding of AAAAABBBBCCCCCCCDDDDEEE (count followed by symbol for each run).
questions.explain: The runs are AAAAA, BBBB, CCCCCCC, DDDD, EEE, giving 5A 4B 7C 4D 3E.

questions.q: Decode the RLE string 3X 2Y 1Z.
questions.explain: 3X = XXX, 2Y = YY, 1Z = Z, so the original is XXXYYZ. RLE is lossless, so decoding gives back the exact original.

questions.q: How many characters long is the string AAAAABBBBCCCCCCCDDDDEEE?
questions.explain: 5 A + 4 B + 7 C + 4 D + 3 E = 23 characters.

questions.q: If each character takes 7 bits, how many bits does the string AAAAABBBBCCCCCCCDDDDEEE take?
questions.explain: 23 characters x 7 bits = 161 bits. At 8 bits per character it would be 184 bits, which is where the range of about 161 to 184 bits comes from.

questions.q: RLE takes AAAAABBBBCCCCCCCDDDDEEE from about 161-184 bits down to about 55 bits. Roughly what fraction of the original size is that?
questions.explain: 55/161 is about 0.34 and 55/184 is about 0.30, so the result is roughly a third of the original.

questions.q: RLE-encoding the string ABCDE gives 1A1B1C1D1E. What does this show?
choices: RLE only saves space when the data contains repeated runs
RLE is lossy, so some characters were thrown away
RLE always halves the size of its input
RLE cannot encode letters, only pixel colors
questions.explain: With no runs, every symbol needs a count added, so the output is longer than the input. Compression only pays off when there are patterns to exploit.

questions.q: Why does a simple black-and-white pixel image (like a heart drawn on a grid) compress well with RLE?
choices: Each row is mostly long runs of the same color
Black and white pixels need no bits to store
Images are always lossy, so pixels can be dropped
Each pixel is encrypted before it is sent
questions.explain: A row looks like 'many white, a few black, many white...'. RLE stores how many pixels of each color in a row instead of every pixel one by one.

questions.q: In which type of compression can the original data be perfectly reconstructed?
questions.explain: Lossless compression (e.g. ZIP) allows a perfect rebuild of the original. Lossy compression (e.g. JPEG) removes some data for good.

questions.q: Which kind of compression must be used for text files and executables?
choices: Lossless, because the original must be rebuilt exactly
Lossy, because text files are mostly redundant data
Lossy, because executables must be as small as possible
Either one, since both rebuild the original exactly
questions.explain: Lossless compression is essential for text files and executables. Losing even a little data would corrupt the text or break the program.

questions.q: JPEG images are an example of which of these?
questions.explain: JPEG is lossy: less important or redundant image data is removed entirely to make the file smaller.

questions.q: ZIP files use lossy compression, so some of the original data is lost.
questions.explain: ZIP is lossless: the original files can be perfectly reconstructed. JPEG is the lossy example.

questions.q: When is lossy compression desirable or permissible?
choices: When reducing size matters more than retaining quality
When every bit of the original must be kept exactly
When sending executable programs between systems
When the data has already been encrypted at Layer 6
questions.explain: Lossy compression throws away less important or redundant data. That is acceptable when a smaller size matters more than full quality, as with photos.

questions.q: The RLE encoding 5A 4B 7C 4D 3E is lossless: the original string can be rebuilt exactly from it.
questions.explain: Each count and symbol tells you exactly how to rebuild the run, so AAAAABBBBCCCCCCCDDDDEEE comes back unchanged.

questions.q: What is a 'session', as managed by the Session Layer?
choices: A single, continuous exchange of data between two devices
A single packet sent from one device to another
The physical cable connecting two devices
A web page retrieved with one HTTP request
questions.explain: Layer 5 manages the session between two communicating devices, meaning a single, continuous exchange of data.

questions.q: Which question does authentication answer?
choices: What are you allowed to do?
Who gets to talk, and when?
What format is the data in?
questions.explain: Authentication verifies the identity of a user or device. Authorization asks 'What are you allowed to do?'.

questions.q: Which question does authorization answer?
choices: What are you allowed to do?
Who gets to talk, and when?
What format is the data in?
questions.explain: Authorization checks the permissions of a user or device. Authentication (identity) normally comes first.

questions.q: Before letting a user delete a file, a system checks that the user has permission to delete files. What is this?
questions.explain: Checking permissions (what the user is allowed to do) is authorization.

questions.q: Before a session starts, a device has to prove who it is with a password. What is this?
questions.explain: Verifying identity ('Who are you?') is authentication.

questions.q: Negotiating a session may involve which of these?
choices: Agreeing on the structure of the conversation
questions.explain: Session negotiation can include authentication (who are you?), authorization (what may you do?) and the structure of the conversation (who talks, and when?). Translation and compression are Presentation Layer jobs.

questions.q: What is full duplex communication?
choices: Both endpoints can communicate at the same time
Only one endpoint communicates at a time, taking turns
Two devices share one session but only one can send
Data is sent twice so that errors can be detected
questions.explain: Full duplex lets both endpoints communicate simultaneously. Half duplex allows only one at a time, so they take turns.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of full duplex communication?
choices: One side talks while the other must wait
questions.explain: On a phone or video call both people can talk at once. A walkie-talkie, where each side says 'over' and the other waits, is a classic half duplex example.

questions.q: In half duplex communication, only one endpoint communicates at a time, so the endpoints must take turns.
questions.explain: That is the definition of half duplex. Full duplex lets both sides communicate at once.

questions.q: At the Session Layer, the choice between full and half duplex depends on the physical medium (the wire), not on the protocol.
questions.explain: It is the other way around. The Layer 5 duplex decision is based on the protocol, not on the physical medium. It is an agreement about how the conversation will run.

questions.q: Most modern devices permit concurrent (full duplex) communication.
questions.explain: Most modern devices allow both endpoints to communicate at the same time.

questions.q: A web browser uses HTTP to fetch a web page. Which OSI layer does this protocol belong to?
questions.explain: HTTP, FTP, SMTP and SSH are Application Layer protocols. Web browsing is an Application Layer service.

questions.q: Data is converted from ASCII to EBCDIC so an older IBM system can read it. Which OSI layer handles this?
questions.explain: Data translation is a Presentation Layer responsibility.

questions.q: Two devices agree that only one of them will talk at a time. Which OSI layer handles this?
questions.explain: Negotiating the terms of the conversation, such as half vs. full duplex, is done at the Session Layer.

questions.q: A user connects with SSH to run commands on a remote machine. Which OSI layer does SSH belong to?
questions.explain: SSH is an Application Layer protocol that provides the remote access service. Its traffic is encrypted, but SSH itself is still classed at Layer 7.

questions.q: An image is shrunk with JPEG compression before it is sent. Which OSI layer handles this?
questions.explain: Data compression, lossless or lossy, is a Presentation Layer responsibility.

questions.q: A server verifies a device's identity before starting a continuous exchange of data with it. Which OSI layer handles this?
questions.explain: Authentication is part of negotiating a session, which happens at the Session Layer.
